text: Every factory air compressor logs pressure, temperature and motor current. Yet air leaks, the most common compressor fault, are usually found only when the line stops. This is Compressor Maintenance Copilot, built by team gheware for the AMD Developer Hackathon.
In a small or mid-sized factory, one maintenance lead looks after many machines. Nobody watches the sensor data, and the manual and past repair notes sit unread when a fault hits.

Our copilot works in two steps. A statistical detector learns what normal looks like and raises an alert. An Evolus workflow then hands that alert to an Evolus agent. The agent searches a knowledge library of the manual and past work orders, and it thinks with DeepSeek V4 Flash, an open model running on AMD GPUs through AMD Token Factory. Our own code checks every answer before anyone sees it.

This is real data from a metro train's air compressor. The detector learned normal behaviour from February and March only. On the twenty-sixth of May, the anomaly score jumps above the alert threshold, three days before the air leak recorded on the twenty-ninth.

One click asks the agent. It explains what is happening in plain words: far more compressor starts and lower reservoir pressure, the air-leak pattern in the manual. It names the likely cause, lists the checks to run in order, and drafts the work order with the parts to have ready.
Every answer cites its sources, so the lead can open the manual section and the past work orders it relied on.
The technician can ask follow-up questions. What did we do last time? The agent finds the two past work orders, a worn check valve and a stuck drain valve, and what was replaced.
Ask whether the machine can keep running until the weekend, and the copilot gives the evidence but never makes that call. That decision belongs to the maintenance lead.
These safety rules run in our code, not only in the prompt. Citations must be real documents. Safe-to-run verdicts are removed. Low confidence goes to a person.

On the four air leaks the operator recorded that year, the detector warned before three of them, from fourteen hours to more than two days ahead, with about one false-alert episode a week. The alert threshold was never tuned on the failures.
The same Evolus agent is also published as a website widget, the way a plant would put it on its intranet, answering from the same knowledge library.

Every model call runs on AMD GPUs. Evolus orchestrates them through three building blocks that our app drives over the REST API: a knowledge library, an agent on our own model, and a workflow. Because the agent thinks on our AMD-hosted model, Evolus spends no credits on reasoning.
The same flow works on a second machine. On milling-machine data with labelled failures, the copilot catches about three in four failures, and close to nine in ten of its alerts are real.

Next is a pilot on one plant's compressors, with its own manual and repair history. Compressor Maintenance Copilot: an early warning, a plain explanation and a ready work order, before the line stops. The code is open source under the MIT licence.
